The SOP should focus on preventing drug, alcohol and substance use among children through regular awareness programmes in schools. Children should be educated about the harmful effects and risks of addiction in simple language. Teachers and parents should be trained to identify early warning signs and provide support. Children affected by substance use should receive confidential counselling, medical treatment and rehabilitation instead of stigma or punishment. Easy access to child-friendly helplines and reporting systems should also be provided. Strong coordination among schools, families and authorities can help protect children from substance abuse and trafficking.

In India, substance abuse among children is becoming a serious concern, affecting not only their health and education but also their future. Children may be drawn towards drugs due to peer pressure, family problems, neglect or simply the easy availability of such substances. What may begin as curiosity or an attempt to fit in can gradually become a serious problem. From a legal perspective, children need more than punishment. Articles 21, 39(e) and 39(f) of the Constitution emphasise their dignity, safety and healthy development. The NDPS Act, 1985 addresses illegal drugs and trafficking, while the Juvenile Justice Act, 2015 focuses on care, protection and rehabilitation. Therefore, while those who supply or exploit children must be held accountable, children affected by substance abuse should receive proper counselling, treatment and support to rebuild their lives.

Children who are out of school and living with their families have no clear place in the draft. The pathway is built mostly around schools. 2. Anyone who reports a seller or a child being used as a carrier needs protection. Drug networks can harm people, and if reporting puts you at risk, people will stay silent. A reporter who keeps getting pulled into court will not report a second time. 4. The draft sets no timeline for NDDTC, AIIMS to develop the treatment and assessment protocols, though training in schools depends on them. I have also pointed out a few inconsistencies in the draft that should be fixed before it is finalised.

Schools and communities should provide children with awareness about the harmful effects of drugs and substance use. Early identification, counselling, family support, and easy access to professional help should be strengthened. The focus should be on prevention, rehabilitation, and protecting children from stigma and discrimination.

To strengthen the NCPCR draft SOP on preventing substance use among children, a robust, child-centric approach is essential. Early prevention must enforce strict 100-meter tobacco-free zones around educational institutions and mandate regular vendor inspections. Teachers, community health workers, and parents require mandatory training for early identification, backed by confidential, non-stigmatizing reporting channels. Response and treatment must prioritize dedicated pediatric de-addiction centers and trauma-informed counseling, treating affected children strictly as victims rather than offenders. Rehabilitation should focus on social reintegration through uninterrupted schooling, vocational training, and peer mentorship to prevent relapse and societal stigma. Finally, seamless inter-agency coordination between CWC, NCORD, school committees, and law enforcement is vital to dismantle illicit trafficking networks while fully safeguarding child rights.

The proposed framework should focus on prevention, early identification, timely treatment, rehabilitation, and reintegration while keeping the best interests and dignity of every child at the center. Schools should have regular age-appropriate awareness programs, trained counselors, and confidential mechanisms for reporting substance-related concerns. Parents and communities should be educated to recognize early warning signs and respond without stigma or punishment. Strong coordination among schools, healthcare institutions, police, Child Welfare Committees, District Child Protection Units, and NGOs is essential. Children affected by substance use or trafficking should receive accessible medical care, psychological support, education, legal assistance, and long-term follow-up. Special attention should be given to vulnerable children and those exposed to trafficking or unsafe environments. The framework should also include regular monitoring, staff training and adequate resources.

The SOP should adopt a child-centric, preventive, and rights-based approach** that addresses both substance use and the risks of illicit trafficking. Schools, parents, communities, healthcare providers, police, Child Welfare Committees, and District Child Protection Units should have clearly defined roles and coordination mechanisms. Early identification should be strengthened through age-appropriate awareness, confidential screening, trained counselors, and safe reporting channels without stigma or punishment. Children affected by substance use should receive timely medical care, psychological counseling, family support, rehabilitation, education continuity, and reintegration services. Special attention should be given to vulnerable children, including those exposed to trafficking, homelessness, poverty, or unsafe environments. The framework should ensure confidentiality, informed participation, regular follow-up, and easy access to child-friendly grievance mechanisms.

Non-Criminalization Policy: Ensure children struggling with substance dependency are treated strictly as victims needing care under the JJ Act, avoiding penal action. Harm Reduction & Medical Support: Provide medically supervised detoxification programs tailored specifically for adolescent physiology. Family & Aftercare Counseling: Implement mandatory family counseling sessions during rehab to build supportive home environments and prevent relapse. Confidentiality Protocols: Strictly protect the identity and medical history of recovering children to safeguard their educational and social future.

Trained teachers, counsellors and Child Protection Officers can identify warning signs and connect children to appropriate psychological, medical and social support. A child asking for help should never have to fear being labelled. I suggest that the SOP create a confidential “Early Help, Not Stigma” pathway in schools, child-care institutions, and primary health settings. A child should be able to privately report substance-related pressure, experimentation, exposure, or fear even before dependence develops and receive a timely assessment and appropriate support without automatic punishment or public disclosure. A trained nodal person should connect the child with counselling, healthcare, family support or rehabilitation when required, with follow-up after referral. The system should record the support provided and outcomes, not simply count how many children were identified. Prevention should begin at the first warning sign, while protecting the child’s dignity and future.

The SOP should recognize that children increasingly encounter substance-related content, peer influence and potential exploitation through digital platforms. NCPCR could promote a Safe Digital Spaces for Children initiative comprising age-appropriate digital education, anonymous counselling, verified information and easy referral to professional support. Interactive games, short videos, quizzes and regional-language content could teach children how to recognize manipulation, peer pressure, online drug promotion and trafficking risks. A confidential chatbot or helpline could allow children to ask questions without immediately identifying themselves. The framework should also include digital-literacy training for parents and teachers so they can recognize online risks while respecting children's privacy and avoiding excessive surveillance.

A confidential Child Recovery Passport could be introduced for children receiving treatment or rehabilitation for substance use. With appropriate consent and privacy safeguards, it could record essential information such as treatment history, counselling needs, educational status, rehabilitation goals, follow-up appointments and referrals. The child should not have to repeatedly explain their circumstances when moving between hospitals, rehabilitation centres, schools or districts. Access should be restricted to authorized professionals, with strong data-protection measures. The passport should focus on recovery and rights rather than criminal history. A portable continuity-of-care mechanism would be particularly useful for children who relocate between caregivers, districts or institutions during treatment and rehabilitation.

The SOP should establish an Early Warning Child Protection Network connecting schools, teachers, counsellors, parents, Anganwadi workers, ASHA workers, Child Welfare Committees and District Child Protection Units. Instead of waiting for a child to develop serious substance-use problems, trained frontline personnel should be able to identify early behavioural, educational, social and emotional indicators and confidentially refer the child for assessment. A simple, child-friendly referral protocol and digital dashboard could help track whether support has actually reached the child. The system should strictly avoid labelling or punishing children, ensuring that early identification leads to counselling, protection and appropriate care rather than stigma or disciplinary action.

The framework should focus on early identification, counselling and timely support for children affected by drug and substance use. Schools, parents and local authorities should be encouraged to identify warning signs and provide help without creating fear or stigma. Easy access to counselling, healthcare and rehabilitation should be ensured, along with proper follow-up and support for children to return to education and normal social life. The approach should be child-friendly, preventive and focused on rehabilitation rather than punishment.

Drugs & Substance Use Among Children (Joint Action Plan 2021) 1. Prevention & Surveillance: Mandate digital surveillance & strict geotagging for pharmacies within a 100m radius of educational institutions. Integrate anonymous, student-led digital peer support "Prahari Clubs" into school safety protocols. 2. Trauma-Informed Screening: Banish punitive measures (suspension/rustication) for children identified with substance use. Implement non-punitive psycho-social diagnostic tools for teachers and counselors. 3. Pediatric Infrastructure: Prohibit placing minors in adult de-addiction or rehab wings. Establish state-funded, child-friendly pediatric detoxification and psychiatric facilities. 4. Restorative Justice: Treat child victims strictly as "Children in Need of Care & Protection" (CNCP) under the JJ Act, bypassing standard police lockups. 5. Aftercare: Mandate 24-month post-rehab monitoring with vocational support, mental health checks, and flexible school re-enrollment.
